Exact moments of order statistics

Source: R/os_moments.R
os_moments.Rd

Computes the means \(\alpha_i = E[X_{(r_i)}]\), the variances and the covariance matrix \(B_{ij} = \mathrm{Cov}(X_{(r_i)}, X_{(r_j)})\) of the order statistics \(X_{(1)} \le \dots \le X_{(n)}\) of an i.i.d. sample of size n from a continuous distribution, at the ranks ranks, by numerical evaluation of the exact integrals, or from a closed form where the family has one. The distribution is one of thirteen built-in families, given as in R by its name and its parameters, or a distribution that the user defines with os_dist.

Usage

os_moments(
  n,
  ranks = seq_len(n),
  dist = "norm",
  ...,
  os_shift = 0,
  os_multiplier = 1,
  cov = TRUE,
  method = c("auto", "integrate", "closed"),
  rel.tol = 1e-11,
  check = TRUE
)

Arguments

n

The sample size, an integer \(\ge 1\).

ranks

The ranks, strictly increasing integers in \(1, \dots, n\). The default is every rank, which gives the full covariance matrix.

dist

The distribution: the name of a built-in family, "norm", "unif", "exp", "logis", "gumbel", "t", "cauchy", "gamma", "chisq", "beta", "lnorm", "weibull" or "f", or an object made by os_dist.

...

The parameters of a built-in family, under the names and with the defaults of R's own distribution functions (the table in Details), for example mean and sd for "norm", shape and rate for "gamma", df for "t". A parameter without a default in R must be given. Nothing is passed here when dist is an object made by os_dist().

os_shift, os_multiplier

The constants \(a\) and \(b > 0\) of \(Y = a + bX\). The function returns the moments of the order statistics of \(Y\), where \(X\) has the distribution that dist and its parameters give: the means become \(a + b\,\alpha\) and the covariances \(b^2 B\). They serve where the distribution has no parameter of its own for a shift or a multiplier: a \(t\) distribution with a location and a scale, a shifted exponential, a three-parameter gamma, Weibull or lognormal, or a user's distribution.

cov

TRUE for the full covariance matrix, FALSE for the means and the variances only, which need single integrals and no double integral.

method

"auto" takes the closed form where the family has one and the quadrature elsewhere, "integrate" forces the quadrature, "closed" requires a closed form for every requested quantity and stops otherwise.

rel.tol

The relative tolerance of the quadrature. The single integrals and the inner integral of a product moment run at rel.tol, the outer integral at 100 * rel.tol.

check

Whether to run the run-time checks of the Details and warn when a residual exceeds \(10^{-6}\).

Value

An object of class "orderStatMoments", a list with the components n, ranks, alpha (the means, named by rank), var (the variances), B (the covariance matrix, NULL when cov = FALSE), quad_err (the summed error estimates of the quadrature, see Details), standard (a list with the alpha, var and B of the standard member of the family, which os_blue reads), dist (the os_dist object of the standard member), par (the parameters of a built-in family, NULL for a user's distribution), os_shift, os_multiplier, affine (the shift and the multiplier that carry the standard member to \(Y\), which combine the family's own parameters with os_shift and os_multiplier), cov, method, route ("closed", "integrate" or "mixed"), checks (the residuals of the run-time checks, NA where a check did not apply) and call.

Details

The built-in families. A family is given as in R: dist is the name that R's functions carry after p, d and q ("gamma" for pgamma), and its parameters are passed by R's own names. Every argument of os_moments() after dist is given by its full name.

distParameters, with R's defaultsClosed forms returned by method = "auto"
"norm"mean = 0, sd = 1none
"unif"min = 0, max = 1every mean, variance and covariance
"exp"rate = 1every mean, variance and covariance
"logis"location = 0, scale = 1the means and the variances
"gumbel"location = 0, scale = 1the mean and the variance of the maximum
"t"dfnone
"cauchy"location = 0, scale = 1none
"gamma"shape, and rate = 1 or scalenone
"chisq"dfnone
"beta"shape1, shape2none
"lnorm"meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1none
"weibull"shape, scale = 1none
"f"df1, df2none

The Gumbel is in the maximum form, \(F(x) = \exp(-e^{-(x - \mathrm{location})/\mathrm{scale}})\), and is the one family that R does not provide. The noncentral versions of the \(t\), the chi-square, the beta and the \(F\) (R's ncp) are not built in, and df1 of the \(F\) must be finite. The package computes the moments of the standard member of each family, the member whose shape parameters are those given and whose other parameters are at R's defaults, and applies the remaining parameters afterwards, exactly: the mean and the standard deviation of the normal, the ends of the uniform, the rate of the exponential, the gamma's rate or scale, the Weibull's scale, and \(\exp(\mathrm{meanlog})\) of the lognormal are a shift and a multiplier of the standard member. A distribution with a large mean or a small rate therefore loses no digits.

The integrals. With cdf \(F\), density \(f\) and \(y < z\), $$f_{r:n}(x) = \frac{n!}{(r-1)!\,(n-r)!} F(x)^{r-1} \{1 - F(x)\}^{n-r} f(x),$$ $$f_{r,s:n}(y, z) = \frac{n!}{(r-1)!\,(s-r-1)!\,(n-s)!} F(y)^{r-1} \{F(z) - F(y)\}^{s-r-1} \{1 - F(z)\}^{n-s} f(y) f(z),$$ and the moments are $$\mu_{r:n} = \int x f_{r:n}(x)\,dx, \qquad \mu^{(2)}_{r:n} = \int x^2 f_{r:n}(x)\,dx, \qquad \mu_{r,s:n} = \int\!\!\int_{y < z} y z f_{r,s:n}(y, z)\,dy\,dz,$$ with \(B_{ij} = \mu_{r_i, r_j:n} - \alpha_i \alpha_j\). The integrals are evaluated by adaptive quadrature (integrate). The numerical design has three parts.

What is computed. The integration is in standardized units of the standard member, \(t = \{x - Q(1/2)\}/\tilde\sigma\), where the spread \(\tilde\sigma\) is the interquartile range divided by that of the standard normal (so \(\tilde\sigma = 1\) for the normal). The absolute tolerances and the cut points then mean the same for a distribution on any scale. Each moment is taken about the center of its own order statistic, \(c_r = Q(p_r)\) with \(p_r = r/(n+1)\), so that a variance is not the small difference of two large moments: taken about the median, the variance of the uniform minimum kept seven digits at \(n = 1000\) and none at \(n = 10^5\).

How it is integrated. The range is cut at \(c_r \pm h_r\), with \(h_r = d_r + 4/\sqrt{n+1}\), \(d_r = 10 s_r / f(c_r)\) and \(s_r = \sqrt{p_r(1-p_r)/(n+2)}\), so that the narrow peak of the order statistic's density at large \(n\) lies inside one piece whose ends the adaptive rule sees. The second term is a minimum half-width. The first moment, whose integrand changes sign, is cut at \(c_r\) as well, and the outer range of a product moment is cut at the points of both ranks. The absolute tolerances are scaled to the width \(d_r\) of the order statistic. A piece that the integrator flags is accepted only when its error estimate is negligible, and the computation stops otherwise (see "What stops with an error").

How the integrand is evaluated. The integrand is assembled on the logarithmic scale, from lbeta(), the log-tails p(x, log.p = TRUE) and p(x, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) and the log-density, so that the powers of the tails never underflow. The difference \(F(z) - F(y)\) is formed on the side where the two numbers are small, so that nothing cancels.

A density that is infinite at an endpoint. A gamma, a chi-square, a Weibull, a beta or an \(F\) distribution with a shape below 1 has a density that grows like \(e^{a - 1}\) in the distance \(e\) from a finite endpoint of its support. Next to such an endpoint the package integrates in the variable \(v = e^a\), in which the integrand is bounded. The distance from the endpoint is then the integration variable itself, so an order statistic that sits far closer to the endpoint than the centered variable \(t\) can resolve is still placed. The range is also cut around the peak of the order statistic in that variable. The package's tests assert the result against exact values: the minimum of a million observations from a beta(a, 1) at \(a = 0.5\), 0.1 and 0.05, within \(10^{-10}\) for the mean and \(10^{-9}\) for the variance in relative terms, and the covariances next to the endpoint at \(n = 1001\) within \(10^{-7}\). For a built-in family \(a\) is the family's own shape. For a user's distribution whose density is infinite at a lower endpoint, \(a\) is estimated from the distribution function, and the endpoint should be at 0, where the distance is represented without rounding. The upper endpoint of the beta is treated in the same way through the reflected variable \(1 - X\). For a user's distribution with an infinite density at an upper endpoint, the reflected variable is not available: the order statistics next to that endpoint are computed less accurately (about \(10^{-10}\) for the maximum of a beta(1/2, 1/2) supplied through os_dist() at \(n = 100\)), and the computation stops once they concentrate against the endpoint. Such a distribution is better supplied reflected, with the endpoint at 0.

The moment condition. A moment is computed only if it exists: with the tail indices \((\nu_L, \nu_U)\) of the distribution, \(E|X_{(r)}|^2 < \infty\) if and only if \(\nu_L r > 2\) and \(\nu_U (n - r + 1) > 2\), and a rank that fails stops the computation with an error. The indices of the built-in families are set by the package: \((\mathrm{df}, \mathrm{df})\) for "t", \((1, 1)\) for "cauchy", \((\infty, \mathrm{df2}/2)\) for "f", and infinite for the others, which always pass. The median of five Cauchy observations has a variance, and the minimum and the maximum have no mean.

The error estimate. quad_err is the sum of the error estimates that integrate() reports for the single integrals and for the outer integrals of the product moments, in the units of the standard member. It is an estimate, not a bound: the inner integral's estimate is not carried into the outer one, and the errors of the means are not propagated into the covariances. The accuracy evidence is the agreement with the closed forms, the identities and the printed tables, documented in the package's tests.

Accuracy at large n. With method = "integrate", the means and the variances of the uniform and the exponential at the minimum, the quartiles, the median and the maximum agree with their closed forms to within \(10^{-9}\) in relative terms at \(n = 10^4\), \(10^5\) and \(10^6\), and so does the correlation of every pair of them, in absolute terms. Up to the relative errors of the two variances, the relative error of a covariance is the error of its correlation divided by the correlation, so the covariance of two nearly independent order statistics keeps fewer digits: the two extremes, whose correlation is of order \(1/n\), keep five to ten significant digits of their covariance at those sizes, depending on the distribution and on \(n\). The package's tests assert the variances and the covariances of adjacent ranks at \(10^{-9}\) and the extremes' covariance at \(10^{-3}\) beyond \(n = 10^4\). A distribution as heavy-tailed as the lognormal with sdlog = 2 is accurate to about \(10^{-9}\) in relative terms rather than \(10^{-11}\), because the far tail of the inner integral of a covariance is resolved at a fixed tolerance. These are the cases that were measured, not a bound for every distribution.

What has been tested. The tests cover three groups of cases. (1) The normal, uniform, exponential, logistic and Gumbel distributions: the closed forms of the last four at sample sizes up to 1001, the identities on full covariance matrices up to \(n = 100\), the printed tables of the literature, and the large samples of the paragraph above. (2) The other eight families at ordinary parameter values: the minimum, the quartiles, the median and the maximum at sample sizes up to 1001, at the ranks whose variance exists, against an integral in the probability scale that uses none of the package's integrands, and the identities on full matrices at \(n = 10\) and 25 for the distributions that have a variance. (3) Cases that were chosen because they are hard. The first kind is a density that is infinite at an endpoint. Gamma, chi-square, Weibull, beta and \(F\) distributions with \(a\) from 0.8 down to 0.05 were run at sample sizes up to \(10^6 + 1\). The beta(\(1/K\), 1) and beta(1, \(1/K\)) distributions, whose moments are exact finite products, were run for \(K\) from 2 to 40 (\(a\) down to 0.025), at sample sizes from \(10^3\) to \(10^7\) and at ranks from the extreme to \(0.999 n\). The beta(\(1/K\), 0.8) distribution, whose density is infinite at both endpoints, was run for \(K\) from 20 to 100 next to its lower endpoint, and its reflection, the beta(0.8, \(1/K\)) distribution, for \(K\) of 20 and 30. The second kind is a variance that barely exists: a \(t\) distribution with 1.005 to 3 degrees of freedom and an \(F\) distribution with df2 from 4.02 to 6, at the ranks where the variance exists and at sample sizes up to \(10^6 + 1\). In group (3) the package was asked for the mean and the variance of 25898 order statistics. It returned 25595 of them, each within \(10^{-9}\) of its reference (a variance in relative terms, a mean relative to the larger of the mean and the standard deviation of its order statistic), and it stopped with an error for the other 303. Of those, 206 have a variance that rounds to 0 in double precision, and 67 are beta distributions that are refused when they are built (see "What stops with an error"). A variance below the smallest normal double, \(2.2 \times 10^{-308}\), is returned to the precision of a subnormal number only, about three digits at \(10^{-320}\). Of 594 covariances next to an endpoint with an infinite density, at sample sizes from 1000 to \(10^6\), the package returned 590, each within \(10^{-9}\) of its exact value in units of the correlation (the error divided by the two standard deviations) and in relative terms, and it stopped for four. The largest sample size in these tests is \(10^6 + 1\), apart from the beta(\(1/K\), 1) and beta(1, \(1/K\)) distributions, which were run up to \(n = 10^7\).

What stops with an error. The quadrature follows the peak of each order statistic's density and the tails of the distribution. It does not follow a second mode: for a mixture of two narrow normals, the mode that holds a tenth of the mass fell between the nodes, and the moments came back as those of the other mode. The package therefore integrates the density of every order statistic it computes by quadrature and stops when the mass is not 1 within \(10^{-7}\), naming the rank and the mass it found. It also stops when a piece of the range cannot be resolved. This happens for a moment that does not exist when the tail indices of a user's distribution were not declared, for a tail so heavy that the mass of the integrand lies far out (the covariances of a lognormal with sdlog = 3 or of a Weibull with shape = 0.2), for the covariance of an extreme order statistic whose variance barely exists (the minimum of 20 observations from a \(t\) distribution with 2.05 to 2.3 degrees of freedom), and for a variance that comes out zero or negative. A beta distribution whose second shape is below about 0.03 can be refused when it is built, with a message that p and q disagree: its median lies so close to 1 that the rounding of the median moves the distribution function, and the two cannot be checked against each other there. Its order statistics are one minus those of the beta distribution with the two shapes exchanged, taken at the ranks \(n + 1 - r\), which the package computes. A wrong number is never returned knowingly. Extreme cases cannot be checked exhaustively, and further development can address the most difficult of them.

The run-time checks. For a symmetric distribution and a rank set closed under \(r \mapsto n + 1 - r\), the means are antisymmetric and the second moments symmetric about the median, which the integrators do not impose; the product moments are then computed for the pairs with \(r + s \le n + 1\) only and reflected. For a complete rank set, the order statistics are a permutation of the sample, so \(\sum_r \alpha_r = n E[X]\), \(\sum_r \mu^{(2)}_{r:n} = n E[X^2]\) and \(\sum_{r,s} B_{rs} = n\,\mathrm{Var}(X)\) for any distribution with a finite second moment, and for the normal (recognized by its functions pnorm, dnorm and qnorm, not by its name) every row of \(B\) sums to \(\sigma^2\) as well. The residuals are stored in checks, in the standardized units of the integration, so that the threshold means the same on every scale, and a residual above \(10^{-6}\) raises a warning, as does a covariance matrix with a negative eigenvalue beyond rounding. The checks detect some failures of the quadrature and do not certify its accuracy: a failure that every integral shares, such as a peak missed in the same way at every rank, can satisfy them.

Cost. A single integral takes a fraction of a millisecond and a double integral a few hundredths of a second. When the covariances are not closed forms, a full matrix needs one double integral per pair, \(n(n-1)/2\) of them, halved for a symmetric family.

References

Wu, Z. and Tong, T. (2026). orderStatMoments: Exact means, variances, and covariances of order statistics in R. Manuscript. The computation, its verification and the comparison with other software.

Royston, J. P. (1982). Algorithm AS 177: Expected normal order statistics (exact and approximate). Applied Statistics, 31(2), 161-165.

Examples

m <- os_moments(5)            # all ranks of n = 5, standard normal
m$alpha
#>            r1            r2            r3            r4            r5 
#> -1.162964e+00 -4.950190e-01  5.413025e-29  4.950190e-01  1.162964e+00 
m$B
#>            r1        r2        r3        r4         r5
#> r1 0.44753407 0.2243310 0.1481477 0.1057720 0.07421527

os_moments(20, ranks = c(1, 5, 10, 20), dist = "exp", rate = 0.5)
